newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Central banks upbeat but warn of economic pitfalls.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Central banks upbeat but warn of economic pitfalls.

text.p: Inflation has been subdued and growth looks promising, but central bankers warned on Monday that the global economy still faced pitfalls that could put a sudden end to the boom on financial markets.

The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said it saw danger lurking in such things as U.S. inflationary pressures that may be difficult to tame; a possible abrupt end to the U.S. expansion; market turbulence in Europe or weakness in Japan's financial sector.

"I am not looking forward to a world in which it is steadily onwards and upwards forever without a pause. Clearly there will be a pause, but the assessment broadly speaking is positive," William White, chief economic adviser to BIS, told a news conference at the bank's annual meeting.

To ensure lasting financial stability and not just low inflation, central banks want to enlist market discipline and banks' own interests in upgrading internal systems and better managing assets, BIS general manager Andrew Crockett said.
"Therefore there would be a lessened reliance on safety nets provided by governments with the inevitable moral hazard consequences they bring with them," Crockett said.

In his speech to the 67th annual meeting of BIS, the world's oldest international financial institution, president and chairman Wim Duisenberg said the challenges ahead were particularly difficult because markets are increasingly global and past safeguards could not assure financial stability.

"Perhaps the most pressing concern is that inflationary pressures in the United States may prove more difficult to tame than is now anticipated and the expansion may eventually end abruptly," Duisenberg said.
This could produce tighter monetary policy and have a big impact on stock prices and other, riskier financial instruments.

"The question is whether the macroeconomic risks have been correctly valued and factored into asset prices or whether the materialisation of any of them could trigger some broader form of retrenchment," he added.
"If not, the search for higher yields...could easily turn into a widespread search for enhanced protection should bad news emerge from whatever source," BIS added in its annual report.

While central bankers have learned the long-term damage that can arise from lax fiscal policies and inflation, BIS's White admitted there were many things that central bankers did not fully understand, and this was an important message in itself.
"There are limits to what everybody knows and in consequence behaviour should be somewhat more prudent and perhaps somewhat less demanding of governments," White said.
The challenge for central bankers is to find mechanisms that safeguard monetary and financial stability amidst continuing deregulation, technological change and innovation, BIS said.

This means that cooperation among financial market supervisors has to be improved across geographical and institutional borders. Public dislosure also has to be improved and regulation made more market-friendly.
Financial institutions also had to be better managed, BIS said, recalling that trading losses at major firms had gone undetected for years.
"Nevertheless, individual and market discipline cannot ultimately be effective if agents act on the expectation of insulation from losses in the event of distress," Duisenberg said.

"At the very least, reconciling prudential safeguards with this philosophy (of free markets) calls for a reduction in the compass of the overly generous safety-net arrangements that, de jure and especially de facto, have operated for so long in a number of segments of the financial industry," BIS said in its report.

The headway made in monetary policy in recent years is largely due to the growing political and social consensus over the merits of price stability and the willingness of governments to give central banks a mandate to fight inflation.

"In the short term, industrial countries' inflation is expected to remain generally subdued and growth, on balance, to strengthen, as those economies less advanced in the cycle catch up," Duisenberg said.
"Similarly, the overall growth and inflation prospects in the non-industrial world are very positive," he added.
The only problem with continuing low inflation was that people might forget the cost of inflation and once again seek to push demand beyond sustainable limits.
But just as it would be premature to declare inflation dead, BIS cautioned it would be unwise to assume that sound economic fundamentals guaranteed good performance.

In addition to BIS' concern about U.S. inflationary pressure, it noted risks from the need for structural reform in Europe, turbulence in the run-up to a single European currency and continuing weakness in the Japanese financial sector.
In Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe the challenge was to restore competitiveness without inflation picking up.
"The fact that banking systems in many of these countries are quite fragile is clearly another source of uncertainty about the macroeconomic outlook," BIS added.
